item.title: Initial Treatment for Acute Low Back Pain and Risk of Opioid Use Disorder and Overdose
item.description:
Importance: Guideline-discordant care for acute low back pain (aLBP) is common and has been associated with adverse outcomes.

Objectives: To estimate the incidence of new opioid use disorder (OUD) or overdose diagnosis among opioid-naive patients with Medicaid coverage initiating treatment for aLBP and to evaluate the association between initial treatment modalities and subsequent risk of OUD or overdose diagnosis.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used data from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2019, with 13 months of follow-up (1-month exposure assessment followed by 12 months of outcome follow-up) from the Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System Analytic Files from 25 states that expanded Medicaid under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act by 2014. Participants included opioid-naive, adults aged less than 65 years who received pain treatment within 1 month of diagnosis of aLBP. Data were analyzed from March 1, 2025, to July 31, 2026.

Exposures: Initial pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatments for aLBP.

Main outcomes and measures: OUD or overdose diagnosis, defined using diagnostic codes for opioid abuse, opioid dependence, opioid-involved overdose, or a prescription for medication for treating OUD.

Results: In this cohort of 399 500 Medicaid patients who initiated treatment for newly diagnosed aLBP, the median age was 39 (IQR, 30-50) years, and 237 846 (59.5%) were female. The cumulative incidence of OUD or overdose diagnosis was 1.4% at 7 months and 2.3% at 13 months. Initiating vs not initiating higher-dose opioids (>50 mg of morphine equivalent) as part of the initial treatment was associated with the greatest risk, increasing risk of OUD or overdose by 146.6% (95% CI, 121.5%-171.7%). Initiating vs not initiating lower-dose opioids prescribed for more than 7 days or gabapentinoids each increased risk by 105.2% (95% CI, 89.0%-121.4%) and 101.6% (95% CI, 84.9%-118.2%), respectively. Nonpharmacologic, noninterventional therapies were associated with reductions in risk of OUD or overdose diagnosis. Initiating vs not initiating chiropractic care was associated with the largest relative risk reduction, decreasing risk by 32.8% (95% CI, 26.8%-38.9%), and initiating physical therapy was associated with 31.1% decreased risk (95% CI, 22.1%-40.1%).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, nonpharmacologic, noninterventional treatment was associated with reductions in risk of OUD or overdose diagnosis while initiating treatment with opioids or gabapentinoids was each associated with higher risks. These results support guideline recommendations favoring nonpharmacologic treatments as first-line therapy for aLBP.

item.title: Timeliness of Emergency Care for Intracerebral Hemorrhage Compared With Acute Ischemic Stroke
item.description:
Importance: Clinical data comparing time to presentation and stroke quality metrics for intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and acute ischemic stroke (AIS) are limited. Understanding these differences is essential to provide timely care to all stroke subtypes.

Objective: To compare prehospital and emergency department (ED) process quality metrics between patients with ICH and AIS.

Design, setting, and participants: Cohort study included patients with AIS and ICH admitted to Get With The Guidelines (GWTG)-Stroke participating hospitals from January 1, 2015, to June 30, 2024, who arrived by emergency medical services (EMS). Data were analyzed from 195 hospitals across the US.

Main outcomes and measures: Prehospital-based and ED-based process metrics (eg, EMS prenotification, door to ED physician assessment time, door to initial brain imaging order) were assessed. Logistic and linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for patient demographics, medical history and presenting factors, and hospital characteristics. Temporal trends of prehospital care metrics were examined.

Results: A total of 195 659 patients (median [IQR] age, 74.0 [63.0-83.0] years; 97 978 [50.1%] female; 31 464 with ICH and 164 195 with AIS) from 195 hospitals were included. The median (IQR) National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 14 (6-23) for ICH vs 6 (2-13) for AIS (absolute standardized difference, 0.694). ICH (vs AIS) was associated with higher odds of door-to-ED physician assessment of 10 or fewer minutes after adjusting for patient demographics (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.02-1.14). This association reversed after adding adjustment for medical history and presenting factors (including NIHSS) and hospital characteristics (aOR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89-0.99). This pattern was observed for door to initial brain imaging order of 20 or fewer minutes (demographic-adjusted: aOR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.02-1.16; fully adjusted with medical history and hospital characteristics: aOR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.85-0.97). Median last known well to arrival time increased by 32.5% for AIS (151 to 200 minutes; P < .001) and 34.3% for ICH (108 to 145 minutes; P < .001), while rates of EMS prenotification largely remained stable for both ICH and AIS.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of patients with acute stroke, patients with ICH arrived at the ED faster but were less likely to achieve care targets. In the context of emerging hyperacute ICH therapies and bundled care models, addressing these differences is essential to optimizing acute stroke outcomes.

item.title: Mortality Among People With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Importance: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with adverse life outcomes and increased mortality. Clarifying the magnitude of mortality risks using international data and the potential association between medication and mortality is essential to inform clinical care and motivate public health strategies to address mortality.

Objectives: To examine the association between ADHD and all-cause and cause-specific mortality and to assess whether mortality risk differs according to ADHD medication use.

Data sources: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, EMBASE, MEDLINE, and CINAHL was conducted from database inception to July 8, 2025.

Study selection: Eligible studies included quantitative research across all age groups reporting all-cause and/or cause-specific mortality in individuals with ADHD, defined via diagnostic criteria, self-identification, trait measures, or ADHD polygenic risk scores. Exclusion criteria were nonoriginal research, qualitative studies, non-peer-reviewed publications, and studies not reporting mortality outcomes.

Data extraction and synthesis: Data extraction was conducted independently by 2 reviewers. Study quality was assessed by 1 reviewer. Summary data were extracted from published reports, and pooled hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated using random-effects model meta-analysis.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and cause-specific mortality (suicide, unintentional or intentional injury, and natural causes), measured using HRs with 95% CIs.

Results: Nineteen studies including 15 920 970 participants (36.1% female) were included. ADHD was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.31-2.24; P < .001). Significant associations were also observed for suicide (HR, 1.89; 95% CI, 1.21-2.95; P = .005), unintentional or intentional injury (HR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.22-2.00; P < .001), and natural-cause mortality (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.16-1.38; P < .001). ADHD medication use in people with ADHD was associated with reduced all-cause mortality (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.64-0.87; P < .001). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies.

Conclusions and relevance: In this systematic review and meta-analysis of ADHD and mortality, ADHD was associated with increased mortality across multiple causes; and ADHD medication was associated with a decreased all-cause mortality risk, underscoring the importance of timely diagnosis and treatment. However, the heterogeneity observed across studies highlights the need for standardized methods and improved control of confounding factors to better characterize mortality risk among individuals with ADHD.
